segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, and on its horns ten diadems, and on its heads blasphemous names.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The beast I saw was like a leopard, its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of its heads looked as if it had been slaughtered to death, yet its fatal wound was healed. The whole earth followed the beast in amazement,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they worshipped the dragon because he had given authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was given a mouth speaking great boasts and blasphemies, and it was given authority to act for forty-two months.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling, those who dwell in heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was allowed to make war on the holy ones and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all who live on the earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered from the foundation of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone has an ear, let them hear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone is for captivity, into captivity they go; if anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed. This calls for the endurance and the faith of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It exercises all the authority of the first beast before its eyes, and it makes the earth and those who live on it worship the first beast, whose fatal wound was healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to the earth before people’s eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It leads astray those who live on the earth because of the signs it was allowed to perform before the eyes of the beast, telling those who live on the earth to make an image for the beast, which has the wound of the sword and yet lived.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast could even speak and could cause all who would not worship the image of the beast to be killed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It causes everyone, the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves, to be given a mark on their right hand or on their forehead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can buy or sell except the one who has the mark: the name of the beast or the number of its name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This calls for wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a person; and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.

notes.phrase: a beast rising out of the sea
notes.traditional: a beast rising out of the sea
notes.note: The description draws on Daniel 7, where four beasts come up out of the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a ten-horned monster, standing for successive empires. Here their features are combined into a single creature. Most interpreters take it as a picture of imperial power, with Rome as its first-century form.

notes.traditional: wounded to death / seemed to have a mortal wound
notes.note: Most translations smooth this to ‘wounded’ or ‘a mortal wound’. The Greek uses the same verb, in the same form, that describes the Lamb ‘as though slaughtered’ in 5:6 and again in verse 8 of this chapter. The beast is presented as a counterfeit of the Lamb, with its own death and recovery, and keeping one English word lets the reader see that.

The passive ‘was given’ (rendered ‘was allowed’ before a verb) recurs through the chapter, in verses 5, 7, 14 and 15. It is usually understood as a reverent way of saying that the beasts act only within limits God permits. The dragon’s grant of power in verse 2 is stated separately and in the active voice.

Forty-two months is three and a half years, the same span as the 1,260 days and the ‘time, times and half a time’ elsewhere in Revelation (11:2–3; 12:6, 14). The figure comes from Daniel (7:25; 12:7), where it marks a limited period of oppression of God’s people.

‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’.

The Greek word here is the same one this translation renders ‘Gentiles’ where the non-Jewish peoples are meant. In Revelation’s fourfold formula ‘tribe and people and language and nation’ the scope is the whole world, so ‘nation’ is used.

notes.phrase: from the foundation of the world
notes.traditional: the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world
notes.note: The translation follows the Greek word order, in which the phrase sits next to ‘slaughtered’. It can equally be attached to ‘written’: ‘whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered’. Revelation 17:8 has that sense without ambiguity, and many scholars and translations read this verse the same way. Opinion is divided.

notes.phrase: by the sword they are to be killed
notes.traditional: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword
notes.note: The manuscripts vary considerably here. Many read ‘if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed’, a warning of retribution. SBLGNT follows the reading of Codex Alexandrinus, in which both halves speak of a fate to be accepted, echoing Jeremiah 15:2. That reading is harder Greek, and most textual critics think it gave rise to the others.
The Greek word covers both trust and faithfulness. Paired here with ‘endurance’ under persecution, it may well mean loyalty that holds firm, and some translations render it ‘faithfulness’.

The word was used for a stamped or engraved impression, such as a brand, the impress on a coin, or an official seal on a document. In Revelation it is the counterpart to the seal placed on the foreheads of God’s servants (7:3; 14:1). Whether a literal mark is envisaged or a symbol of allegiance is disputed.

The Greek can mean the number of a particular human being, which fits a name to be worked out, or ‘a human number’, meaning one reckoned in the ordinary human way (compare ‘a human measure’ in 21:17). The translation takes the first sense, which is the more common view.

A few early witnesses read 616, a variant already known in the second century, but 666 is much better attested. Greek and Hebrew letters doubled as numerals, so a name could be ‘calculated’ by adding up its letters. The most widely held solution is ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew letters, which gives 666, or 616 in a spelling closer to the Latin form. The identification is not certain.

candidates.reason: It ranges from bowing in homage before a superior to worship of a deity, and translators split between ‘worship’, ‘bow down’ and ‘pay homage’, with theological weight in the Gospels and Revelation.
It recurs across Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation, and varies in English between ‘patience’, ‘endurance’, ‘perseverance’ and ‘steadfastness’.

It is a theme word in Revelation and the Johannine letters, rendered variously as ‘conquer’, ‘overcome’ and ‘be victorious’, and the link between the beast’s conquering and the believers’ conquering is lost if the English varies.
It occurs throughout the New Testament and is rendered ‘authority’, ‘power’ or ‘right’; it needs to be kept distinct from δύναμις (‘power’), which stands beside it in this chapter.
‘Sign’ and ‘miracle’ are both common renderings, and the word is thematically central in John’s Gospel and in Revelation, so it should not vary.
